category.title: Design-Oriented Data Structures
category.description: Designing efficient data structures by combining multiple structures to support real-world operations with optimal time and space complexity.

algorithms.title: Min Stack
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(1) for push, pop, top, and getMin
algorithms.summary: A stack that can return the minimum element in O(1) time.
explanation: Normal stack gives push, pop, and top in O(1).
The extra problem is finding the minimum quickly.
We can maintain another stack called minStack.
minStack stores the minimum value seen so far.
Whenever we push a value, we also update minStack if the new value is smaller.
When we pop, we remove the value from both stacks.
This makes getMin() O(1).

exampleTrace.input: push(5), push(3), push(7), getMin(), pop(), getMin()

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Find the minimum element of a stack without scanning the whole stack.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When stack operations and minimum queries happen frequently.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Expression processing, monitoring systems, interview problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: The minimum is maintained during insertion, so no extra scan is needed.

algorithms.title: Max Stack
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(1) for push, top, and peekMax; O(log n) for popMax with ordered structure
algorithms.summary: A stack that can also return and remove the maximum element efficiently.
explanation: A normal stack only knows the top element.
For maximum queries, we need another structure to track maximum values.
A max stack can use a stack plus an ordered structure.
The stack keeps insertion order.
The ordered structure helps find the maximum quickly.
When popMax is required, we locate the maximum and remove it.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Provides normal stack operations plus maximum-element operations.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When both LIFO access and maximum queries are required.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Priority-aware stacks and interview design problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: A second ordered structure avoids scanning the entire stack.

algorithms.title: LRU Cache
algorithms.summary: A cache that removes the least recently used item when it becomes full.
explanation: LRU means Least Recently Used.
Suppose a cache can store only 2 items.
If we access one item, that item becomes recently used.
When the cache is full and a new item arrives, we remove the least recently used item.
HashMap gives O(1) lookup.
Doubly linked list gives O(1) insertion and removal.
The combination of HashMap and Doubly Linked List gives O(1) get and put.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Keeps only recently used items when cache capacity is limited.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Browser cache, API cache, database cache, memory cache.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Operating systems, databases, web servers, distributed systems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: HashMap gives direct lookup and doubly linked list gives O(1) recency updates.

algorithms.title: LFU Cache
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(1) average for get and put
algorithms.summary: A cache that removes the least frequently used item.
explanation: LFU means Least Frequently Used.
Every item has a frequency count.
When an item is accessed, its frequency increases.
If the cache is full, we remove the item with the smallest frequency.
If multiple items have the same frequency, we usually remove the least recently used one.
A HashMap stores keys.
Another map connects frequency to a doubly linked list.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Removes rarely used cache entries instead of simply removing old entries.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When access frequency matters more than only recency.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Frequency buckets allow finding the lowest-frequency items efficiently.

algorithms.title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1)
algorithms.summary: A structure supporting insert, delete, and random element retrieval in O(1) average time.
explanation: A hash set gives O(1) insert and delete but does not support random access.
An array gives O(1) random access but deleting an arbitrary element can be O(n).
Use both an array and a HashMap.
The map stores value -> index.
To delete, swap the target with the last element.
Then remove the last array position.
This avoids shifting elements.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Combines fast lookup, deletion, insertion, and random selection.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When all four operations need to be fast.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Random sampling, game systems, randomized testing.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Array provides random access and HashMap provides O(1) index lookup.

algorithms.title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1) With Duplicates
algorithms.summary: An extension of Randomized Set that allows duplicate values.
explanation: Duplicates make deletion harder.
A single value cannot point to only one index.
So the map stores value -> set of indexes.
The array stores all values.
During deletion, replace the removed element with the last array element.
Update the index sets accordingly.

traceSteps: Remove one 5 by swapping with last element

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Supports duplicates while keeping insert, delete, and random operations fast.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When duplicate values are allowed.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: The index set lets us find one occurrence without scanning.

practiceProblems.title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1) - Duplicates allowed

algorithms.title: Design HashMap
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(1) average for put, get, remove
algorithms.summary: Build a HashMap without using a built-in hash table.
explanation: A HashMap converts a key into an array index using a hash function.
Different keys can produce the same index.
This is called a collision.
One simple solution is chaining.
Each bucket stores a list of key-value pairs.
For get or remove, we search only inside that bucket.

traceSteps: Both values are stored in bucket 1.
get(1) searches bucket 1 and returns A.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Stores key-value pairs with fast lookup.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Whenever direct key-based access is required.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: A good hash function spreads keys across buckets.

algorithms.title: Time Based Key-Value Store
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(log n) for get and O(1) amortized for set
algorithms.summary: Stores multiple values for a key at different timestamps and returns the latest valid value.
explanation: A key can have many values.
Every value is associated with a timestamp.
For get(key, time), we need the value with the largest timestamp less than or equal to time.
Store timestamps in sorted order.
Binary search finds the correct timestamp quickly.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Retrieves historical values efficiently.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When data changes over time and old versions matter.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Configuration systems, versioned data, event history.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Sorted timestamps allow binary search.

algorithms.title: Find Median from Data Stream
algorithms.summary: Maintains the median while numbers arrive one by one.
explanation: The median is the middle value after sorting.
Sorting every time would be expensive.
Use two heaps.
Max-heap stores the smaller half.
Min-heap stores the larger half.
Keep their sizes almost equal.
Then the median can be read directly from the heap tops.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds the median of a growing stream without sorting everything again.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Real-time statistics and streaming data.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Two heaps maintain the middle values dynamically.

algorithms.title: Trie / Prefix Tree
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(L) for insert, search, and prefix search
algorithms.summary: A tree designed specifically for fast prefix-based string operations.
explanation: A Trie stores words character by character.
For example, cat and car share the path c -> a.
Each node contains links to next characters.
A word-ending marker tells us where a complete word ends.
Search and prefix operations depend mainly on word length, not number of stored words.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Fast word and prefix searching.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Autocomplete, dictionary lookup, prefix matching.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Search boxes, IDE autocomplete, spell checkers.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Each character is processed once.

algorithms.title: Autocomplete System
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(L + K log K) depending on ranking implementation
algorithms.summary: Uses a Trie and ranking information to suggest words while the user types.
explanation: Autocomplete starts with a prefix.
A Trie quickly finds the node representing that prefix.
From that node, we can explore possible words.
Each word can also store a frequency or popularity score.
The highest-ranked matching words are returned.
This combines Trie, DFS, and ranking.

traceSteps: Sort by popularity and return suggestions.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Provides search suggestions as a user types.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Search boxes and command interfaces.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Trie avoids scanning every stored word.

algorithms.title: All O(1) Data Structure
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(1) average for increment, decrement, getMinKey, getMaxKey
algorithms.summary: Maintains key frequencies while supporting minimum and maximum frequency queries in O(1).
explanation: Each key has a count.
We need to increase and decrease counts.
We also need the key with minimum count and maximum count.
A HashMap stores key -> frequency node.
A doubly linked list keeps frequency groups in sorted order.
Each frequency node stores all keys having that frequency.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Maintains dynamic frequencies with constant-time min/max access.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When frequency updates and extreme-frequency queries are both frequent.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Frequency buckets are connected directly through a doubly linked list.

algorithms.title: Hit Counter
algorithms.summary: Counts events that happened within a recent time window.
explanation: Suppose we want the number of hits during the last 5 minutes.
We do not need old events forever.
A circular array can store counts for each second.
Each position represents one time slot.
When the slot is old, overwrite it.
This is a common time-window data structure.

traceSteps: At time 3 -> all three hits are inside the window.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Counts recent events efficiently.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Monitoring and traffic tracking.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Old time slots can be reused instead of storing unlimited events.

algorithms.title: Logger Rate Limiter
algorithms.summary: Allows a message to be printed only once during a fixed time interval.
explanation: Store the last timestamp when each message was printed.
When a new message arrives, check its previous timestamp.
If enough time has passed, allow it.
Otherwise reject it.
A HashMap is enough for this problem.

traceSteps: At time 2 -> only 1 second passed -> reject.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Prevents repeated messages from being processed too frequently.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Logging, notifications, duplicate-event prevention.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Only the latest timestamp for each message is required.

algorithms.title: Snapshot Array
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(log n) for get, O(1) amortized for set and snap
algorithms.summary: Stores versions of an array so an old snapshot can be queried later.
explanation: Normally changing an array destroys its old value.
Snapshot Array keeps historical versions.
Instead of copying the entire array on every snapshot, store only changes.
Each index keeps a list of (snapshotId, value).
For get, binary search finds the latest change before the requested snapshot.

traceSteps: The value in snapshot 0 is still 5.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Provides historical versions without copying the whole array.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Versioning and undo/history systems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Only changed values are stored.

algorithms.title: Range Sum Query Mutable
algorithms.summary: Supports updating an array value and finding the sum of a range efficiently.
explanation: If we calculate a range sum by looping every element, it can be O(n).
When many updates and queries happen, this becomes slow.
A Fenwick Tree can maintain prefix sums.
An update changes a few tree positions.
A range sum can be calculated using two prefix sums.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Supports range sum queries with dynamic updates.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Large arrays with many updates and range queries.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Fenwick Tree reduces both operations to O(log n).

algorithms.title: Segment Tree
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(log n) update and range query
algorithms.summary: A tree that stores information about ranges and supports fast updates and queries.
explanation: A Segment Tree divides an array into smaller ranges.
Each tree node represents one range.
For example, the root may represent the whole array.
Its children represent the left and right halves.
Queries visit only the ranges that are necessary.
This makes dynamic range operations efficient.

traceSteps: Segment Tree combines the required nodes.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Fast range queries with updates.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When Fenwick Tree is not flexible enough for the required operation.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Each operation touches only O(log n) tree levels.

algorithms.title: Disjoint Set Union
algorithms.summary: Maintains groups of connected elements and efficiently merges groups.
explanation: DSU is also called Union-Find.
Each element belongs to a group.
find tells us which group an element belongs to.
union combines two groups.
Path compression makes find faster.
Union by size or rank keeps the tree shallow.

traceSteps: find(3) returns the representative of this group.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Tracks connected components while edges are added.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Dynamic connectivity and grouping problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Path compression and union by size make operations almost constant time.

algorithms.title: Priority Queue / Heap
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(log n) insertion and deletion, O(1) peek
algorithms.summary: Maintains the most important or highest-priority element at the top.
explanation: A normal queue processes elements in arrival order.
A priority queue processes elements according to priority.
A heap is commonly used to implement it.
In a min-heap, the smallest value stays at the top.
In a max-heap, the largest value stays at the top.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Efficiently retrieves the highest-priority element.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Scheduling, top-K problems, shortest path.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Heap keeps the extreme element at the root.

algorithms.title: Deque
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(1) insertion and deletion from both ends
algorithms.summary: A double-ended queue that supports operations from both front and back.
explanation: A deque allows insertion and deletion from both ends.
It can behave like a stack or a queue.
This makes it useful in sliding-window problems.
A deque can also maintain candidates in increasing or decreasing order.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Provides efficient access from both ends.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Sliding windows, queues, stacks.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Both-end operations are constant time.

codeTemplates.code:
from collections import deque

dq = deque()
dq.append(1)
dq.append(2)
dq.appendleft(0)
dq.pop()
print(dq)

algorithms.title: Monotonic Stack
algorithms.summary: A stack maintained in increasing or decreasing order to solve next greater or smaller element problems.
explanation: A monotonic stack keeps values in a fixed order.
For a next greater element problem, we can maintain a decreasing stack.
When a larger value arrives, smaller values can be removed.
Every element enters and leaves the stack at most once.
Therefore the total work is O(n).

traceSteps: 1 is smaller than 2, so both stay.
3 arrives and is greater than 1 -> next greater of 1 is 3.
3 is also greater than 2 -> next greater of 2 is 3.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds next greater, next smaller, previous greater, or previous smaller values efficiently.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When the problem asks about the nearest greater or smaller element.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Each element is pushed and popped at most once.

algorithms.title: Monotonic Queue
algorithms.summary: A deque that maintains values in sorted order to answer sliding-window maximum or minimum queries.
explanation: Suppose we need the maximum of every window of size k.
Checking every window separately can take O(nk).
A monotonic decreasing deque keeps the largest useful element at the front.
Elements that can never become maximum are removed.
Each element enters and leaves once.
Therefore the entire process is O(n).

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Answers sliding-window maximum or minimum queries efficiently.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Large arrays with fixed-size sliding windows.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Every element is processed a constant number of times.

algorithms.title: Circular Buffer
algorithms.summary: A fixed-size queue where the end connects back to the beginning.
explanation: A circular buffer has a fixed capacity.
When the end of the array is reached, we wrap around to index 0.
Two pointers can track the front and rear.
This avoids shifting elements.
It is useful when memory size must remain fixed.

exampleTrace.input: capacity=3, enqueue(1), enqueue(2), dequeue(), enqueue(3), enqueue(4)
traceSteps: Insert 4 wraps around to the free position.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Implements a fixed-size queue without shifting elements.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Streaming systems and fixed-memory queues.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Array positions are reused through circular indexing.

codeTemplates.code:
class CircularBuffer:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.buf = [None] * capacity
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.head = 0
        self.tail = 0
        self.size = 0

    def enqueue(self, x):
        if self.size == self.capacity:
            return False
        self.buf[self.tail] = x
        self.tail = (self.tail + 1) % self.capacity
        self.size += 1
        return True

    def dequeue(self):
        if self.size == 0:
            return None
        x = self.buf[self.head]
        self.head = (self.head + 1) % self.capacity
        self.size -= 1
        return x

algorithms.title: Design Twitter Feed
algorithms.timeComplexity: O((F + T) log F) for feed generation
algorithms.summary: Combines hash maps, sets, lists, and heaps to build a social-media news feed.
explanation: Each user can post tweets.
Users can follow other users.
A feed should show recent tweets from the user and followed users.
A HashMap stores tweets for each user.
A Set stores follow relationships.
A heap can merge recent tweets from multiple users.

exampleTrace.input: User 1 follows User 2. User 2 posts A. User 1 posts B.
traceSteps: Feed considers tweets from users 1 and 2.
Newest tweet B appears before A.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Builds a feed from multiple users while keeping posts ordered by recency.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Social feed and timeline design problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: A heap efficiently merges sorted tweet streams.

algorithms.title: Design File System Using Trie
algorithms.summary: Represents hierarchical file paths using a Trie-like tree.
explanation: A file system contains paths such as /home/user/docs.
Each directory is a node.
The next directory is a child node.
This naturally forms a tree.
A HashMap inside each node allows fast child lookup.

traceSteps: Inside a, create directory b with value 2.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Stores hierarchical paths and associated values.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Whenever data has a tree-like path structure.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Each path component is processed once.

algorithms.title: Range Module
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(log n) to O(n) depending on interval structure
algorithms.summary: Tracks intervals and supports adding, removing, and querying whether a complete range is covered.
explanation: A range module stores intervals such as [10,20).
Adding a new range may merge overlapping ranges.
Removing a range may split an existing interval.
Query checks whether every point in a range is covered.
Ordered intervals or a Segment Tree can be used.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Maintains dynamic covered and uncovered ranges.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When intervals are repeatedly added, removed, and queried.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Ordered intervals avoid checking every individual point.

algorithms.title: Design Parking System
algorithms.summary: A simple state-based data structure that tracks available parking spaces.
explanation: There are different parking slot types.
Each type has a remaining capacity.
When a car arrives, check the capacity for its type.
If capacity is available, decrease it and return true.
Otherwise return false.

exampleTrace.input: big=1, medium=1, small=0; add big, add small
traceSteps: Add small car -> no slot available.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Maintains limited resources by category.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Simple resource allocation problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Only a fixed number of counters is needed.

algorithms.title: Key-Value Store with Expiration
algorithms.summary: Stores key-value pairs that automatically become invalid after a specified time.
explanation: Normal HashMap stores values until they are removed.
An expiring key-value store also stores an expiration timestamp.
During get, compare the current time with expiration time.
If the value has expired, return an invalid result.
A HashMap is enough for basic lazy expiration.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Stores temporary data that should automatically expire.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Sessions, temporary tokens, cached responses.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Expiration metadata can be checked directly during lookup.

algorithms.title: Token Bucket Rate Limiter
algorithms.summary: Controls how many requests a user can make during a period using refillable tokens.
explanation: Imagine a bucket containing tokens.
Every request consumes one token.
Tokens are added back over time.
If no token is available, the request is rejected.
Each user can have a separate bucket.
This combines a HashMap with time and counter information.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Controls request traffic so a user cannot send unlimited requests.
wAnswers.whenToUse: API protection and traffic control.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Only token count and last refill time need to be maintained.

codeTemplates.code:
import time

class TokenBucket:
    def __init__(self, capacity, refill_rate):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.tokens = capacity
        self.refill_rate = refill_rate
        self.last = time.time()

    def allow(self):
        now = time.time()
        elapsed = now - self.last
        self.tokens = min(self.capacity,
                          self.tokens + elapsed * self.refill_rate)
        self.last = now

        if self.tokens >= 1:
            self.tokens -= 1
            return True
        return False

algorithms.title: Consistent Hashing Ring
algorithms.summary: Maps keys to servers while minimizing key movement when servers are added or removed.
explanation: Imagine all hash values arranged in a circle.
Each server is assigned one or more positions on this circle.
A key is hashed to a position.
Move clockwise until the first server is found.
If a server is added, only nearby keys need to move.
A TreeMap or ordered map can represent the ring.

exampleTrace.input: Servers A at 10, B at 50. Key hashes to 30.
traceSteps: Therefore key is assigned to B.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Distributes keys across servers while reducing redistribution.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Distributed caching and sharded systems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Adding one server does not require remapping every key.

algorithms.title: Bloom Filter
algorithms.summary: A memory-efficient probabilistic structure for checking whether an item may exist in a set.
explanation: A Bloom Filter uses a bit array and multiple hash functions.
When an item is inserted, several bit positions are set to 1.
When checking an item, those positions are inspected.
If any required bit is 0, the item definitely does not exist.
If all are 1, the item may exist.
False positives are possible, but false negatives are not in a standard Bloom Filter.

exampleTrace.output: cat -> possibly exists, dog -> probably does not exist
traceSteps: Hash cat using multiple hash functions.
Query cat -> all required bits are 1.
Query dog -> if one required bit is 0, dog definitely was not inserted.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Checks set membership using very little memory.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When occasional false positives are acceptable.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Databases, caches, web crawlers, distributed systems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Stores bits instead of complete objects.
